utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Margetts, are you ready to continue the examination-in-chief of Mr. Omeragic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I see Mr. Usher has left already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Omeragic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like you remind you of the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony yesterday. Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts. Examined by Mr. Margetts: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, good morning. When we finished yesterday, we just had just shown a video of your arrival at the municipal building. Now, after you assembled at the municipal building, where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I think -- yes, after that, somebody said there would be no meeting so we went towards the barracks. Fikret Abdic demanded that he meet the refugees that everybody kept talking about and that were said to be in the big barracks of the JNA, so we went there to reach some sort of agreement. Some people were trying to organise our movements. Somebody said, "Go this way," others said, "Go this way," I couldn't understand what was going on. Anyway, we set off towards the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your vehicle leave alone or did other vehicles from the convoy travel with you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only Mr. Abdic's vehicle went there. The vehicle in which I arrived. I couldn't understand what happened to the others. We drove for about 10 or 12 minutes maybe, and then we reached the barracks. There, we got out of the car alone ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Omeragic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Margetts, I would like to understand in what framework the vehicle -- it wasn't said to us at the beginning of the examination of the testimony, in which general framework the cars moved, what was the purpose of this, who decided it? Can our witness answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Going to Bijeljina, sometimes Mrs. Plavsic's car would be the first in the convoy, sometimes Mr. Abdic's car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like you to go back in time further and I would like to understand in what framework this was organised. Was this an inspection mission? Was this meant to visit a place? Who had decided it? Why did you go there? Who went along with you? I would like to understand why you went there officially. Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I can answer this. In Bijeljina on the 1st of April, this conflict happened. There were rumours about victims, casualties, rumours about war. So Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Abdic went there on some sort of a peace mission, as a delegation, to find a way to preserve peace, on a peace mission of some sort. Fikret Abdic was possibly going to go to Bijeljina to see what the situation was like in order to inform the other members of the Presidency, there were six in total. So they were going to Bijeljina and I believe the reason was some sort of attempt to restore peace. There was some footage broadcast on Serbian television where you could see fighting. Mr. Abdic was a member of the six-member Presidency in Bosnia and Herzegovina, he was an elected member, elected at the preceding elections. He enjoyed some authority and I believe he was elected with an overwhelming number of votes. So he enjoyed a lot of authority and a good reputation and he had participated on quite a number of peace missions together with Mrs. Plavsic. They had been to Brod previously and to Derventa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Mr. Abdic asked your boss at your newspaper to be accompanied by some kind of journalist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry. You may have misunderstood my explanation. I was a journalist of this newspaper, Slobodna Bosna. My editor came to me and said, "We have an opportunity to send somebody to Bijeljina and since the chef de cabinet of Mr. Abdic is our friend, I'm just negotiating for somebody from the media to accompany them to Bijeljina, and I volunteered to be the journalist going on that mission representing my newspaper because the other employees of the newspaper were girls and I didn't want them to go. Anyway I volunteered and Mr. Abdic said, "Okay, you will go there as my spokesman," because the situation was qualified as dangerous on all sides and everybody said that Bijeljina was deep in trouble. And when he saw me he said, "You don't really look like a spokesman you look more like a bodyguard." They had to invent some sort of legend for me, some sort of false identity. So I went there as his bodyguard posing as his bodyguard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you were introduced as a bodyguard. Why were you not just introduced as a journalist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps because on the 2nd of April he had an accident that he told me about. It was when the delegation of Bosnia and Herzegovina were stopped at the entrance to Bijeljina and they were told to lie down. As far as I remember Mr. Abdic's story and some other stories, the then-Defence Minister, Jerko Doko, and I believe also the Minister of Justice, Miodrag Simovic, who is today a member of the constitutional court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I forgot to saw that Jerko Doko was a Croat and Mr. Simovic was a Serb. Some other people were there including Mr. Abdic and just before nightfall they tried to go into Bijeljina however, they were not allowed to. This delegation was stopped at the checkpoint held by Arkan's men and they were told to lie down on the road. The problem was there was mud on the road and they were told to lie down. Nevertheless, Mr. Abdic was the only one who didn't want to lie down, and the Arkan appeared from somewhere in the dark and resolved this standoff. Anyway Abdic demonstrated some courage in this incident. However, generally speaking it all testified to the danger that reigned in Bijeljina, and they wanted to have somebody in the delegation who would help find out the real truth and write about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, yesterday you informed the court that the only reason you thought that you were allowed to enter Bijeljina was that you were represented as a bodyguard and not as a member of the Sarajevo press. Following Mr. Abdic's experience that you have just described to the Court, did Mr. Abdic indicate that he did not believe any Muslim journalists would be able to enter Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this really suspect the sort of matter that should be subject to a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will put the question to the witness. Mr. Omeragic, did Mr. Abdic indicate anything at all on how it would be received by others if a journalist would be present during this visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. But, Your Honour, if you allow me. This very fact that I should pose as somebody else was something that Mr. Abdic suggested himself; why, I can only guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you form an opinion on the why, apart from just guessing, of course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe there was some danger involved in going into this place where things were absolutely uncertain; something never seen before had happened. But everywhere in Bosnia it was quite obvious that we were living in a world about to be overwhelmed by war. The streets were blocked. There was unrest in the air.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that journalists were in any way protected in the Bosnian war; on the contrary, I believe they were ultimately forced to take sides without any way of crossing their own lines or going to some other side. I can even give you an example. There was a correspondent of Slobodna Bosna, Trbic; he was very badly beaten and sustained serious bodily injuries in -- and later he was killed. I know of other journalists who kept their jobs, worked at their desks and were killed. Mr. Smajlovic, a journalist of Oslobodjenje newspaper was killed right at the outset of the war; he was killed in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for the transcript, I was too quick with putting my question to the witness. I asked him and he now answered that question whether the danger for a journalist would be any other than for another person, since this does not appear on the transcript. I apologise for that. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, you've referred to the exclusion of the Sarajevo press. The members of the Sarajevo press, predominantly which nationality were they?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my firm conviction that all the ethnic groups were equally represented, roughly speaking, in the press corps, and editors always took care about this issue. For instance, the TV of Sarajevo sent Vlado Mrkic to report from Bijeljina -- sorry, Vlado Mrkic was sent from Oslobodjenje, a Serb, and another Serb was Velibor Golubovic was sent to report for TV Sarajevo, and sometimes nationality was a decisive factor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court why it was that members of the Belgrade press were in Bijeljina but members of the Sarajevo press were excluded?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you a number of reasons why, for instance, representatives of the Belgrade media could go in without any problems at all and do their job, while members of the Sarajevo media were prohibited from doing so. You could say that in Bijeljina -- I saw my colleagues from Politika Express and Politika Belgrade newspapers I saw journalists from Novi Sad, but people from the Sarajevo press were simply unable to freely go into such places, into crisis areas, and report freely, at least at the beginning of the war. In those initial conflicts such as Brod, Derventa, Kupres, journalists of all ethnicities could still go in and report; however, after Sarajevo was blocked and after the rupture of communications, it would never be the same again. The Belgrade press was allowed in probably because the problem with the Belgrade media had been resolved. I believe they had all been put into the service of the Serbian nationalist idea, the Serbian nationalist drive in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and there was nothing to hide from them, whereas from the Sarajevo media you had to take an effort to hide certain things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Omeragic. I'm just going to take you out of chronological sequence. In your previous answer you mentioned Vlado Mrkic. Would you be able to tell the Court whether you met Vlado Mrkic in Bijeljina, and if so, could you describe that meeting to the Court.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Vlado Mrkic from before, from working for the Oslobodjenje newspaper. He was an elderly man by that time. He was around 58, 59 years old. He was a grey-haired man, very lean, and he was known as an extremely objective journalist, a very honest man, very professional. That was his reputation among journalists from Sarajevo. At one point, as we were returning from visiting people in their homes in Bijeljina, there was Mrs. Plavsic, Arkan with his men, and Mr. Abdic and everybody else, to my side, a couple of metres away, I noticed Mr. Vlado Mrkic. I hurried a little to join him, wishing to talk to him, however he gave me a blank stare as if he couldn't remember where he knew me from. So I told him I am from Slobodna Bosna newspaper, from Sarajevo. After that, we started talking. He confessed to me that he had entered from southern side, from Zvornik, using byroads and going around about in order to reach Bijeljina because he was not able to reach Bijeljina using the main road which was dotted with checkpoints. Anyway, we started talking, as I said, and we started discussing very rapidly. He was talking under his breath, expressing his dissatisfaction. He was very upset about the situation in Bijeljina. And suddenly, he raised his voice too much condemning what had been done in Bijeljina. And at one point while walking by Arkan he said almost aloud, everybody could hear him, He said, "You will never be forgiven for what you have done to the Muslims in Bijeljina. History will judge you." At that moment, I was really afraid for him, for what might happen to him. Arkan turned his way, and I think this is the first time I saw him confused and at a loss. Everybody was looking at him at that point, Arkan, Mrs. Plavsic, everybody, and Mr. Mrkic even raised his finger and started saying the same thing again, "Nobody will ever forgive you," and then Arkan said, "Give me your ID." In his ID, Arkan saw Vlado Mrkic, Bijeljina. It was an old ID from the times when he was a correspondent from Bijeljina. And seeing this ID, Arkan said, "So you are a Croat." And then Mrs. Plavsic joined the conversation and said looking with condescension at this honourable, wonderful man she said, "No, he is a Serb, but what kind of Serb?" She may have even said "unfortunate" or something like that. I can't remember exactly. Anyway, Arkan pushed this ID back into Mrkic's hands and said, "Now get lost. Take him away from here." They took him away and I was really scared and worried, worried for him, of course. However, a couple of hours later I saw him in Bijeljina again. He had walked around and around and caught up with us again. I was really happy to see him, to see that everything was all right after all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Omeragic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to play the video excerpt which is Exhibit P300.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The case manager will just distribute the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, just for my information, the CD contains all the video clips we are going to look at?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: As I understood it, Your Honour, we were going to produce a separate CD for each of the video clips. I'll just confer with my case manager to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand this is already in evidence as P300.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And in respect of the others, we will produce a separate CD for each clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "In front of the SDS seat, Ms. Plavsic, former member of the Republic of the -- Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina announced ..."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, you've seen the clip, which is Exhibit P300, which depicts Plavsic kissing Arkan. From viewing that clip, can you tell the Court where that kiss took place?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the kiss in front of the municipality building as we were parting. I visited Bijeljina only on that one day, but I saw the kiss in front of the building of the Bijeljina Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, I see that on the transcript, the text does not appear. Is it a kiss or is it the text what -- and I'm also looking at you, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's only the kiss that's important.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would certainly be objecting to the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Margetts, of course the text is under the clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in this instance it appears that this text has already been admitted as P300, but for this purpose we're not referring to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's just the reporter who says what happened, and that's of course -- whether that's true or not. What we see is first of all --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: First of all, the substance of the evidence, Your Honour, is the video clip, that's what it's sought for. And in terms of what's -- the reporter's indicating as we all know, the first casualty of war is truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, to what extent would the OTP like us to pay attention to the text spoken by the journalist?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with one reservation, and that is that I wasn't the representative of the OTP that presented Exhibit P300, I would indicate that I can't think of any reason why we would want the text to be maintained as part of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a look at what happened when P300 was tendered during the examination of Mr. Kljuic and we'll then further see what to do with the admission at this moment. Apart from -- the text, of course, explains that it is Mrs. Plavsic who kisses Arkan and the remainder of the text is mainly about what the journalist says that happened, which is not shown on the clip itself apart from the clip starting with a body which is -- seems to be the victim of violence but all the rest of the text is not -- does not become clear for the clip itself. So therefore, apart from that this was said during the pictures were shown, apart from that it seems to have no -- it seems not to have any further evidentiary value.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it would be convenient, I may confer with Mr. Harmon during the break and inform the Court of his response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, you just informed the Court that you saw Plavsic kiss Arkan at the time that they were parting following your tour of the municipality. Can you explain to the Court who was present when Plavsic kissed Arkan and how they reacted or behaved in the presence of Arkan?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was some local SDS officials there who accompanied the kiss shouting in approval. This was a sound of approbation and not really wonder, but it was accompanied by an exclamation of approval, I would say. There were Generals Jankovic and Prascevic there as well; I don't know what their reaction to this was as well. Mr. Abdic was there as well and saw the kiss, but there was no reaction whatsoever on his part. Only later a story started going around about this, but I'm afraid I did not really manage to notice what the reaction on the part of those people who were, let's say, prominent among them was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the generals greet Arkan?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the visit, one could see that the generals, Mr. Prascevic and Jankovic, were in a position that seemed to be inferior to that of Mr. Arkan, and one could feel that throughout the visit. When General Prascevic and Arkan greeted, general approached him a couple of steps ahead and then stopped and was quite relaxed, or rather Arkan was -- his demeanour was quite relaxed for a person who held no rank at the time and for a person who, as such, was being approached by a general. Just before we were to depart, as far as I remember, I was some 3 or 4 metres behind, at the rear of the group, as a person who holds no special position would be in such a group. At that point, General Savo Jankovic was seated on a bench and next to the bench, Arkan was pacing to and fro and there was Ms. Plavsic as well, as well as General Prascevic. At one point, Mrs. Plavsic said that now that everything was over, the town should be handed over to the control of the JNA. I don't recall what the exact wording of this request was, but that was the gist of it. In any case, Madam Plavsic was -- termed it as a kind request, but then Arkan said, "No, we haven't quite finished our business yet. We would then go on to Bosanski Brod." And he mentioned Armin Poharic, who was a man number one of the defence of Bosanski Brod. At that point, Arkan threatened that he was going to fuck his mother and deal with him. As he said that he was going to attack Bosanski Brod, General Jankovic merely went with his hands through his hair in dismay and said, "You shouldn't really be talking this way." At that point, I was unable to grasp what sort of a relationship existed among them, as I was trying to analyse what had been said at that time. I even made some inferences of mine - I'm not sure whether this is the right place to really present them to you, but if you'd wish me to, I would gladly do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Omeragic, if you could continue and communicate to the Court, based on your observations during the day, what those inferences were.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: In relation to the matter -- well, Your Honour, inferences are something that the Trial Chamber draws from the evidence; it's not a matter for the witness. The witness can give of what he saw, heard, perceived, what have you, but inferences, I mean that's a very poorly phrased question and it's not the sort of evidence that will assist the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would agree that we do not ask the witness to make any inferences, but of course he could tell us what he thought at that time and whether or not he did form any opinion about that. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, and what the opinions are based on and shared fact and opinion and what have you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So where Mr. Margetts asked to you tell about your inferences, the Chamber would like to know what went through your mind at that time and whether you formed any opinions about the situation. Please proceed. You may answer, then, the question understood in this sense.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I came to certain conclusions, but it was only at a later stage because at that time I felt in danger and did not really have time enough to ponder about it. Upon my return, I gave much more thought to it. The first that came to my mind was that approach by the general which showed to me that the army's position was an absurd one. For a general to approach a person who holds no rank whatsoever and then report to him, that shows the absurdity of the position which the army found itself. I also made some later inferences to the -- to the facts that Arkan had some political clout that had been given to him. I think that he must have enjoyed political support on some very high levels. When you look at also the fact that his army was not the only one to be present there in Bijeljina, you had other paramilitary formations like the White Eagles, Bijeli Orlovi, my line of thinking was as follows. It was as if they wanted to have as their justification the fact that the paramilitaries were there, and in the future they'd be able to blame everything that happened on the paramilitaries rather than on the regular army, and that that was why they allowed them to have their way. These were the sort of conclusions I reached. I tried later on to find answers for all the peculiarities that I noticed, but these are just some of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just in relation to that last answer from line 18 to the end of the answer really does not form anything of the nature of the kind of evidence that the Trial Chamber should be receiving. This is -- that is just the musings of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this type of submission is something that would be appropriate at another stage of this trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think it's appropriate as a marker as the sort of evidence that the Trial Chamber should not be receiving from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I think we're shading from this question of inferences and conclusions and opinions and musings. It's really not appropriate in the form of evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to interrupt my learned friend at this stage. I don't think it's appropriate for her to make this type of commentary on the evidence in the course of the witness giving his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, the line between drawing inferences and telling us what went through the witness's mind is of course rather thin. We'll consider the matter during the next break to what extent and what probative value could such parts of the testimony have and also whether it should be struck from the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That is what my submission is based on, because I want to ensure from the perspective of the Defence that -- and to be of assistance to the Trial Chamber, a line must be drawn between the evidence that a witness can give in relation to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, please --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It's inappropriate for Mr. Margetts to interrupt me --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Could the witness then be excluded from the court whilst this --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, I agree with that. I'm happy for him to interrupt me on that score.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, the Chamber will focus on the facts and any inferences, whether that would be ours as well is of course a matter to decide at a later stage, and the Chamber will focus on the facts and Judge Hanoteau has one additional question for the witness. Mr. Omeragic, would you please listen to a question that will be put to you by Judge Hanoteau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to Mrs. Plavsic, there were two generals and Mr. Arkan. What difference was there in terms of attitude or was there a difference in attitude on the part of the military personnel, the generals, and on the part of Mr. Arkan? Did you -- you spoke in your testimony of a respectful attitude, could you be more specific, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that Arkan dominated the whole situation, and this could be seen in his statements. He was saying that once he will have dealt with all the matters he still had to deal with in Bijeljina, he was going to go on to Bosanski Brod. One could also infer this from General Jankovic's demeanour vis-a-vis Arkan who seemed to approach him as a person who would be of lower rank to him because General Jankovic was telling him when Arkan stated that he was going to go on to Bosanski Brod and slaughter there everyone, he said, "You shouldn't be talking this way."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Plavsic, did the generals have a more deferential, more respective attitude towards her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't possibly remember that detail now. But on our return to Tuzla, one could see officers, General Jankovic and Prascevic, treating her as a lady in a very careful manner, with politeness, thoughtfulness, and they showed respect for her as for a person that held a highly -- high-ranking political position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... that she had authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, she did, definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Authority vis-a-vis the military personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, following on from His Honour Judge Hanoteau's questions, could you describe to the Court the nature of the relationship between Arkan and Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can tell you about this relationship is that Madam Plavsic called Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, "my dear," "my child," which showed of a very close relationship or perhaps a wish for a very close relationship, whereas Arkan on his part showed great respect for her. And one could not fail to notice this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A further question, and I'm sorry to move you once again out of chronological sequence and this time also to move you from Bijeljina to Bosanski Brod; however, were you present when negotiations were taking place in Bosanski Brod and Ms. Plavsic was present and there was shelling of that city?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just in relation to this again, I mean I think it's quite obvious what areas should not be led on and what areas can be led on and it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's split up.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: The questions have to be split up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I would say this is a perfectly appropriate area to lead. I do not know what is contentious about describing the situation

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to find out. Ms. Loukas, is it in dispute that any negotiations were taking place in Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Ms. Loukas, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone please

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now what was the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was about negotiations in Bosanski Brod.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- from Bijeljina to Bosanski Brod. Were you present when negotiations were taking place in Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the first part. Is that in dispute? Is that in dispute?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's -- as far as I'm concerned, Your Honour, the question just shouldn't be asked in that fashion. Which portion is Your Honour asking me whether or not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First let's split up the question. First of all Mr. Margetts takes the witness from Bijeljina to Bosanski Brod which is, I think, perfectly --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I don't have a problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem with that. Negotiations taking place in Bosanski Brod, is there any dispute about whether there were any negotiations taking place in Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't have a problem with that, but as to the presence of Ms. Plavsic, I'm just simply not in a position to know and I don't think it's a matter that should be led on because she's a member of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then ask the witness. Are you aware of any negotiations that took place in Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know who were present or who were involved in these negotiations? Could you tell us who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was again Ms. Plavsic, Franjo Boras, and Fikret Abdic who took part in these negotiations in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. capacity of mediators of some sort, and I remember that taking place in Bosanski Brod. I believe I was present there once for some 45 minutes and nothing really transpired. Nothing was really going on of any substance. If this may interest you, it concerns JNA officers. I recall one occasion when Ms. Plavsic, this was in Derventa close to Bosanski Brod, when shelling started, and at that point I was not present in the meeting. Mr. Abdic and Ms. Biljana Plavsic came out of the meeting room and said, "Let's each call our own lot." I believe Mr. Abdic called Ivan Krzic or some other officer there to have the shelling stop. Ms. Plavsic called commanding officers at the barracks and they were talking to them and saying, "We should each deal with our own side firing." Ms. Plavsic said, "Stop the shelling because we are here negotiating for peace whilst you are shelling citizens." Mr. Abdic, on his part, almost stated the most -- the identical thing saying, "We should make sure that firing stops." Next, as if a miracle happened, there was a respite from shelling and they resumed negotiations, but ten minutes later shelling was resumed again and the same thing happened all over again. There must have been someone on higher positions who was responsible for this. So the same thing happened again, the shelling started, and it is ridiculous for them and absurd for them to go through the same thing again. Therefore , I saw them taking part in the negotiations, trying to resume peace and I could see how powerful they were and what they could do about bringing about peace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, yesterday we were

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we got French translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is sorry, her mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We identified yesterday direct observation and direct involvement of high-level authorities in events happening on the ground to be a sensitive issue. So therefore, I would agree with Ms. Loukas that you could have asked who were present because on the basis of this statement, you could expect that the answer would include a high-level authority. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If the witness could be present with the exhibit which is not listed next in order, that is the fifth listed exhibit being a letter from the Bijeljina SDS to the Main Board of the SDS. And I note in the exhibit sheet that it's noted as being dated 8 April, in fact you'll see that the date that appears on it is 3 April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Prosecution Exhibit P586.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: As that's being distributed, Your Honour, I'd just like to read the content of this facsimile into the record. This is a facsimile from the Municipal Board of the SDS to the SDS Main Board and it reads as follows: "We are requesting that all organs of Serbian Assembly should support the decision of the Crisis Staff of the SAO Semberija and Majevica and of the commander of the Serb National Guard. The entire Serbian people are organised in units at the Territorial Defence in the territory of our region --" there is an illegible word following the word "region" -- "and they expect that the JNA should restrain from the conflict with Serbian people. We are prepared to give arguments for our firm position."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts are you reading from a different translation, although it's approximately the same? The illegible part does not appear in my translation. I've got a translation in front of me last four digits being 6742.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am reading from a different translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Why don't you use the same as you provided to us. I think the gist of the translation is certainly the same, but -- so you may proceed, but if it comes to any detail of the text, then we'd have to move to the same translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I apologise for that. The correct translation which we present as part of Exhibit P586 is the one marked at 6742.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, is the reference in this document --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we proceed, Mr. Margetts has given evidence from the bar table that this particular document, whilst translated as 8th of April, is actually 3rd of April. I must say looking at the photocopy of the document in question in the Cyrillic version, it doesn't appear like a 3 to me and it certainly appears more like an 8. So I don't know if Mr. Margetts proposes to give evidence that the dating of documents, which is very significant --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I referred to the facsimile marker at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, you see that it appears as 03/04/92, 16.54 at the top.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour, but the document itself says 8th of April, and seeing it's a photocopy it's very hard to understand, without having seen the original, what the question of this document -- I have real problems with this document, I must say, Your Honour. It's something that appears on the face of it to say the 8th of April. It's not a little fax header that says the 3rd of April. It's an entirely significant document --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, again my learned friend is making submissions which are appropriate at a different stage of the trial. I think there has now been ambiguity that she has been raised and that's fine, but further submissions are inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I also have a further objection, if I might be permitted to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you have any further objection, please --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you. What light could this witness cast on this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid that if Mr. Margetts explains that, that you might blame him for giving evidence --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, I look forward to hearing it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first wait for his first questions --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and then see whether the witness could tell us anything about that. Ms. Loukas, you've drawn our attention to the fact that you, on the bottom of the page, that you -- I would say that you adhere to the date as we find it in the translation, which is a different date from what we find at the top of the text. And we have to see how important that is and what consequences that might have.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, is the date of any specific importance for the questions to be put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll first listen what questions you will put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, because it's not unknown for fax machines to have the wrong dates on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, at the same time, Ms. Loukas, since you are commenting as well at this moment, and the 8 is not an undisputable 8. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, when you were in Bijeljina on the 4th of April, 1992, what were your observations as to the activity or involvement of the JNA in the events that were taking place in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that I saw the confirmation of the opinion that I had, namely that the JNA was completely isolated in that situation, it was completely set aside, somehow thrown to the sidelines although it was the regular army. Of course they were expected to refrain from conflict with the Serbian people, and the Serbian National Guard took over. Those self-organised organisation were at the forefront and the JNA, the regular army, who were supposed to preserve peace, was on the back burner. And my opinion was confirmed that they were not doing their jobs, that they were watching and waiting to see what will happen. They were completely, as I said, thrown to the sidelines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to interrupt the examination for one second, and that is to inform the Court that the Exhibit P300, which is the video we saw prior to the last exhibit, it went into evidence without the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I now do understand that no transcript is added to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the witness could be shown the next video clip which is the one that appears fourth on the exhibit list and it's 30001462 from the timer marking 1.48.30.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Prosecution Exhibit Number P587, and the transcript will be P587A.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Mrs. Plavsic, you are a member of a mixed delegation which has come to Bijeljina today to see for themselves the alleged destruction of which the Sarajevo media have been reporting extensively. Is that your impression, the first impression?" Answer: "From what I could see travelling through town by car, not only I but my escorts as well were looking carefully to see if we would see shattered glass, shop windows, and so on, the things that we had heard about from the media in Sarajevo. We saw none of that. And somebody even said the shoe shop would be the first to be looted, if anything; however, the shoes were intact in the shop window, we saw them. Therefore, from what I could see when entering the town, I wasn't under the impression that we were entering a plundered and enslaved town, and I am particularly glad that the people received us cheerfully and I am under the impression that the people had a feeling they were saved from a great evil that had been threatening them." Reporter: "I'll ask you one more question. You are a member of a mixed delegation, however other members of the delegation, Fikret Abdic and the army representatives, are not with you here. It's a little strange they went to the barracks first instead of you all being together in the same place so that light can be shed on the whole situation."

utterances.speaker: MRS. PLAVSIC
utterances.text: "You see who was all directed by me. The first barricades I had encountered, one of our MPs at the assembly was at the barricade. He said that I should determine it and the column was much longer. The representatives of the European Union were in this column. Yesterday I said they should not come with us. However, they were waiting for us in Tuzla. Yesterday, I told them that we didn't want them to come with us. So this whole motorcade, very long, started together with us, with the journalists, and I was the first in that motorcade. Of course the general whom we took with us was the first and then the soldiers in his escort, then Mr. Fikret Abdic and his escorts." Reporter: "And why did they go to the barracks first?"

utterances.speaker: MRS. PLAVSIC
utterances.text: "Well, I wanted to come here first to be in direct contact with the Crisis Staff on my own first, and then we will all talk together. And now we are expecting them in order to go to the barracks together." Reporter: "Do you know what is going on in the barracks that they had to go there first?"

utterances.speaker: MRS. PLAVSIC
utterances.text: "No, no, I have no idea. Please let me say there is no ulterior motive; you shouldn't think that. First of all, we came here under military escort and it may have been normal for me to go to the barracks first too. But since I can decide for myself, I decided to go to the Crisis Staff of the Serb people first to meet with Mr. Arkan and his associates, and we are very happy to have met him, including Mr. Goran Adzic. I knew that this close encounter of ours would be better without the rest of the group and then later we can talk with them too."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, I noted that in the translation, the written translation, second page, second block, second line, it says, "You shouldn't think that there are bad intentions there," which was translated now as that an "ulterior motive," which is not exactly the same. I'd like you to perhaps verify this issue. You find the translation on page 28, line 1. I'd like you to clarify but I take it that is not the core of the questions you will put to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we will clarify that. And yes, Your Honour, it isn't the core of the questions we'll put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, Ms. Plavsic refers to Mr. Goran Hadzic. Is he the gentleman sitting on Ms. Plavsic's right with the beard?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I saw him on that video clip.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just for certainty, Mr. Arkan is the man sitting on Ms. Plavsic's left?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court who Mr. Goran Hadzic is.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Goran Hadzic was man number one in eastern Slavonia, an area in eastern Croatia, as far as I know. He was the political leader of the Serbian Autonomous District of Slavonia, eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Plavsic refers to what she observed when she was driving through the town, in particular she refers to the fact she had not seen any broken windows and so on. Can you describe to the Court what you saw in terms of numbers of broken windows or any other evidence of a battle.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any particular signs of battle. I saw some shattered windows. They told me it was the post office. I have to remind the Honourable Trial Chamber that it was my first visit to Bijeljina, but I was told that the building on which I saw a lot of shattered windows was the post office. And I saw broken windows on another building but I can't remember which building it was. So there was that, and there were some holes in the walls that we passed by, some bullet holes in the walls, and also in -- on some trees. Apart from that, I didn't see any particular signs of fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Plavsic states that she saw one of "our MPs" she says at the barricade, did you see any civilian personnel at the Serb barricades?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw some civilians that had found shelter in the shrubbery. They were actually hiding behind some shrubs training their guns at us. I saw them when I looked to my side. They were hiding there in the shrubbery and pointing their guns at our cars. There was also a person of some authority who was talking to Mrs. Plavsic, but I wasn't aware that he was an MP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's also references from Mrs. Plavsic in relation to the Crisis Staff. Whilst you were in Bijeljina, did anyone refer to the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the time, they talked about the municipal hall. Some people referred to the Crisis Staff, however I can't remember who spoke about the municipal hall and who spoke about the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that they referred to the municipal hall and some people referred to the Crisis Staff, why do you bring together those two descriptions, that is municipal hall and Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was the same building, as far as I know. It's just that the municipal hall turned into the Crisis Staff once the Croats and Muslims were excluded from it. It turned into the Crisis Staff. That's probably the explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, I'd now like to take you to the barracks, your arrival at the barracks, and could you describe to the Court what happened whilst you were -- after you arrived at the barracks and whilst you were outside the buildings.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So when we arrived at the barracks, we stopped and officers, soldiers, people in uniform were 10 metres away from us. On three big piles on a big plateau with the big building of the barracks on the right, there were people -- there were three huge groups of people, several hundred, perhaps, some were standing, some were lying. And Fikret Abdic was saying all the time that he wanted to see the refugees, to talk to the refugees. He repeated constantly that he had to meet with the refugees. And I believe we stopped there for a moment. Somebody was talking on a hand-held radio saying that Fikret Abdic had arrived, that he wanted to see the refugees. After a while, we were joined by General Jankovic and we went into the crowd. And this is perhaps what left the greatest impression on me, this crowd of wretched people. General Jankovic told me it was a mixed group including Croats, Bosniaks, and as we went into the crowd, I was close to Fikret Abdic. Suddenly, a woman from this crowd uttered an oath. I turned, and I saw some 40, maybe 50 metres away from me Mrs. Plavsic. She was standing alone. I don't know where her escorts were at that time, and since it was a very juicy oath, somebody was saying to her, "Why the hell aren't you coming over here?" Using an F word. I turned and I felt very embarrassed because of all that. And I looked her way again after a while, but she wasn't standing in the same place anymore. That was the last I saw of her at the barracks. Later, as I was talking to the people from the crowd, I tried to learn about their stories, what brought them there. I talked to one particular woman. I tried to get her to tell me the real truth, but she was very afraid. She was saying horrible, horrible things have happened, but she wouldn't say exactly what. She just said that two of her brothers were killed. I found out their names eventually, those were the first names that I got and I noted them down. Every 20 metres or so, people in olive-green/grey uniforms were standing with their guns, but they were not doing anything. So they were not violent, they were just holding their weapons with their barrels pointed to the ground. So after meeting these people, we went into the building of the barracks, it was very close by, which was where Mr. Jankovic and Mr. Abdic had a meeting while I sat in the room next door. The doors were opened and I thought I could overhear their conversation, however they spoke in very low voices and I couldn't make anything out. From time to time, I would only hear Mr. Abdic saying, "I have to meet with the refugees some more. I have to talk to the refugees some more." And at some point, Abdic was told that Mrs. Biljana Plavsic was waiting for him in the municipal hall, that everybody had already gathered there and were waiting for him. I can't remember whether they talked about the municipal hall or the Crisis Staff at that particular moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, I'm looking at the clock. We are close to 10.30. If you could find a suitable moment within the next two or three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, now is a suitable moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I would first ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. We'll have a break for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Margetts, first of all, the text under the video clip of the interview of Mrs. Plavsic did not develop as the spoken words. I checked in the B/C/S transcript -- the B/C/S audiotape, the B/C/S text could be heard so therefore, we have the French and the English translation complete in the transcript, we have the B/C/S in the audio. So therefore there should be no problem, but perhaps you would pay attention to it that this time, the text not -- is usually scrolled under the video clip. Then I think you should have been a bit more cautious about the 3rd and the 8th of April issue. Of course you could have drawn our attention to it, but just to bluntly state that it was the 8th of April was a bit too much, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in that respect, Ms. Loukas is not a handwriting expert nor am I. What we both can see is that the printed text from the fax machine records the 3rd of April, which does resolve the ambiguity in my submission without any shadow of a doubt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well of course Ms. Loukas made some comment on that, and if you insist on such printed text, then perhaps you should consider as well how a text which clearly in writing says that it's written at 17.50 could by sent by telefax at 16.54. That's one hour before it has been written. That, of course, supports Ms. Loukas's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- submission that these fax machines -- but of course they are also -- of course we could say it's totally logic because one hour difference, wintertime/summertime, so when -- if it's 17.50 would have been 16.50, then 16.54 would be totally logical. The only thing I say is that it's not that easy to draw conclusions and to present them as facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour -- and thank you for that guidance, and I had not engaged in a forensic analysis, not even one that matched Your Honour's own analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just looked at the document, nothing more, nothing less. And perhaps said to Ms. Loukas that the 8 as translated might not be that clearly 8 so therefore, whether it's an 8 or not is still to be considered; and as far as the title line is concerned, it needs some more analysis as well. We'll adjourn until five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... into English again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, after you left the barracks, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We set off in the direction of the Crisis Staff, that is the municipality hall in Bijeljina. We entered the building. There were journalists waiting outside while the others were inside. I remember that as everyone was trying to enter the premises, that they denied access to the TV Sarajevo -- to the Sarajevo TV crew, and I was also banned from entering. There was Arkan there in the doorway saying who was allowed to enter and who wasn't, so I remained in the corridor along with some other people who were escorts of Mrs. Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Omeragic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to play the next video and also display a still from that video after it's been played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Prosecution Exhibit P588, and the transcript will be P588.A.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "They were caught by surprise. You could sit here. This is my place. Bishop Kacevenda is also coming. "Hello, how are you doing?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, you have just stated to the Court that you were excluded from the room. Does this video depict that event?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is me. I'm the tallest person here standing by the door. A minute later I was going to be -- I was approached by Arkan, who told me that I had to leave the room and could not attend the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your colleague Nenad Zamfirovic present, and if so, was he allowed to enter?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was allowed to enter. The only ones left outside was me, journalist Golubovic, and the Sarajevo TV crew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which organisation was Mr. Zamfirovic associated with?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He periodically worked as a correspondent for Slobodna Bosna as a Belgrade correspondent. He was a widely respected journalist and we respected him as a colleague, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What ethnicity was Mr. Zamfirovic?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nenad Zamfirovic is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned before that you waited outside in the corridor. Could you describe to the Court for how long you were outside the municipal hall, and could you just go through the events that took place whilst you were waiting outside.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I just wish to add that behind the door here, there was a corridor where there were several of us -- this was an anteroom 2.5 metres by 2. There was Predrag Vladisavljevic, so I don't know what his last name was, some other escorts, and colleague Golubovic. We were waiting for the meeting to finish; it went on for some 35 minutes. As we were waiting there, one of the Arkan's soldiers arrived; he was wearing a black uniform and what they called an Arkan's cap, a black cap. He asked Golubovic who he was. Golubovic said that he was a TV Sarajevo journalist. This Arkan's man asked whether this was Alija's TV and said some things to slight the journalist. The two men who were with him wore olive-green uniforms, and the Arkan's men told the two to take Golubovic away, which they did; however, there was this one person who ran up to Arkan's -- to the Arkan's men and -- or rather he started whispering something into his ear, and this man I'm talking about was Ms. Plavsic's escort. I could only discern the name Kukanjac. Then this Arkan's man said, "Don't mention this name to me. That's even worse than what you've mentioned before." Some two or three people ran down the stairs, took the journalist out, and this Arkan's man returned right away, approached me, and asked me to show him some ID and inquired after my identity. I was unaware of what was going on. He looked me in the eye and I could -- I was -- I could see that his eyes were wide open. Somebody later told me that he might have been under the influence of drugs because the whites of his eyes were very prominent. I told him that I did not have any ID on me, that I was Mr. Abdic's escort and that I -- my papers were in the car. He said to the other two to take me away. They took me under the arms and then one nice-looking man who was Prascevic's escort, he was as tall as me but seemed stronger than me, broad-shouldered, he told them, "Leave this man alone. Why are you bothered by him here?" Then they asked him who he was and what he wanted. I think he used a derogatory term, because this other man was wearing a green coloured uniform, and then there was a row between the two of them, a spat. The other two men, one of them named Peda Pedja [phoen] held me firmly under my arms and then they started pushing each other, inquiring of one another, Which army do you belong to? Which army do you belong to? They were -- there was an altercation, and obviously there was hostility in the air. Then one of them pulled out a pistol and pointed it against my forehead and I told him, "Put this away. You might accidentally trigger it." At that moment, probably attracted by the noise that we were making, Arkan appeared at the door and asked, "What's going on? What's this noise all about?" Or something to that effect. In doing so, he seemed to have saved me because the other two men let go of me. They all relaxed. Arkan motioned with his hand, meaning to tell us to go away, and the Arkan's men and the other two disappeared. I turned towards Predrag and said, "What's wrong with this -- with these men?" And I thanked him. I was hardly aware of the seriousness of the situation at the time. It was actually later on that I took fright by it all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Omeragic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to play the next video which is next on the exhibit list, which is the segment of V0001462 commencing at 1.55.11, and also there will be a still following that video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Prosecution Exhibit P589, and the transcript P589A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, could you already prepare for all the transcripts still to be seen to be provided to the registrar so that distribution can be more efficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise for that inefficiency. That, in fact, will be the last transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I'm, as always, a bit late. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "How was your journey?" Abdic: "It was good, excellent. Since 6.00 this morning I just shaved and straight to work. First it was Mostar, from Mostar to Derventa, and from Derventa ... and back to Tuzla." Arkan: "And the other general, the commander of the second military district didn't come?" General: "No, he could not due to his commitment, business." Arkan: "Business?" Plavsic: "Since I've been put in charge of chairing this meeting, I'll just a little -- shall we wait for the bishop?" Probably Simic: "No need. The representative of our Crisis Staff will explain how it was envisaged." Plavsic: "No, no. I'm not going to explain the situation." Simic: " ... about the protocol, about the way this meeting --" Plavsic: "Good, good. Somebody said I should chair the meeting. Rather somebody else did." Probably Simic: "This meeting is of an informal nature. Right? Let us get familiarised." Arkan: "Those are Serbs." The anchor: "Arkan is showing photographs of killed Serbs." "Yes, those are photographs of killed Serbs but the TV Sarajevo and Jutel presented it as if they were killed Muslims." "You have nothing against the public?" "No, nothing." "Well, if the journalists are finished, we have the numbers, we know everything. Serb Volunteers Guard is good information." Abdic: "Taken into account the misinformation, there are lots of misinformation, not in this one ... generally it would be good if we checked every source of information thoroughly so that we have accurate information. The way out from these difficulties is having accurate information." Arkan: "I agree. But just one thing. This machine-gun was manufactured for the Muslims. It is painted green. Normally the machine-guns are made black. This one is especially made green for Muslims, made in Croatia. So it's the same story again, the Ustashas have come to Bosnia-Herzegovina to make these things with the help of your extreme Muslims. That's the story. So this Ustasha's chequered board evil." Abdic: "The first information, yes, but let's not evaluate it." Arkan: "No, no. I won't evaluate. I'm just telling you." Abdic: "Information, yes; but the evaluation, no, not in advance. We'll evaluate it after having thoroughly discussed it and checked all the information that we have or will have." Arkan: "Mr. Fikret, it's very clear, crystal clear, that Muslim extremists, that is to say, the imported ethnic Albanians who worked in bakeries and whatnot and who were all armed and ready to subjugate the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Serb people here once more. It's important to note that all of this, all these events for the Serb cause..." Male voice: "We agreed to visit Bosnia..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, whilst the still is being displayed, which it now is, I would like to indicate that in fact Your Honour was well ahead of the Prosecution in regard to the videos. Whilst that was the last segment from video 1462, I've been informed by my case manager that we do have a video to come, that will come at the end of this witness's evidence, and so we will distribute that transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, do you see this still displayed on the screen in front of you? Do you recognise the man in the centre who is standing wearing a black jacket with his hand outstretched?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the man I saw in Bijeljina with curly hair and the outstretched arm. I believe it's written Simic here, but I think that's Ljubisa Savic. At the time, in the news report that I wrote as a result of the visit, I said that this was the man who placed the rifle barrel against my forehead and somebody whispered to me that this might have been Mauzer; however, it was only later that I did establish that this man is Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer. I would like to mention the context here where I met him. There was a man, a member of the Territorial Defence, wearing a green uniform who drops a rifle just as we were leaving the hospital. And the sound of the rifle falling reverberated and then the -- and then Arkan approached the man, slapped him and told him to get away from there because he couldn't be called a soldier even. He said to the others that he should immediately be stripped of his uniform, that he should be demobilised. Just as we were about to leave, we were outside the municipality building, this man, Ljubisa Savic, was playing with the rifle bayonet. He was just in front of me and this bayonet fell to the ground; Arkan turned in his direction. This man turned red in his cheeks and everybody including myself expected Arkan to do something terrible, but he just said to the man to pick the bayonet up. It was evident that this man, Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer, had a position that was rather different from that of an ordinary soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Omeragic. Now, just referring to the video clip that you've just seen, you will have seen that Arkan presents a machine-gun painted green to Abdic and he informs Abdic that the Serb volunteer guard has good information. Abdic responds and refers to misinformation and that every source should be checked. Arkan then says that the machine-gun is manufactured in Croatia for the Muslims. And Arkan continues stating the following, he says, "It is very clear, crystal clear that the Muslim extremists, that is to say, the imported Albanians who worked in baker shops and whatnot and were all armed and ready to subjugate the Serb people here once more." Whilst you were in Bijeljina, did you see anything that supported Arkan's claims that Muslim extremists were ready to subjugate the Serb people?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't see green submachine-guns or anything that would show that Muslims were ready to do anything evil to their Serb neighbours or to subjugate them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to present the next exhibits to the witness, and they're two photos which are Exhibits P294A and P294B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, I can see that you have the photos before you and the one that's furthest to your left, I believe, is the photo with a 08 in the top right-hand corner. Could you look at the soldiers in this picture and tell the Court whether you saw men dressed in the uniforms that these soldiers are wearing whilst you were in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them may have been wearing uniforms like these. But the ones that I saw all had black uniforms and had the sign of a tiger with his muzzle wide open, and it was written underneath "The Serbian Volunteers Guard."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The soldier that appears to be poised in a kicking action, do you recognise the insignia that appears on his right arm?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see the insignia on his right arm and that -- that's the sign belonging to the Arkan's Tigers, the emblem in three colours that I believe reflect the then Yugoslav flag without the five-pointed star. And I believe that there, there's also an image of a tiger with his jaws wide apart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, did you see men in camouflage uniforms whilst you were in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember seeing any difference in the colour of the uniforms. I can't remember whether there were any but most of the soldiers wore these black uniforms, including the insignia of the Serbian Volunteers Guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst you were in Bijeljina, were you able to distinguish between different military groups, or did you consider that all of the military personnel were within one group?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three types of uniforms. There were the ones worn by Arkan's men, which were black, and some of them may have had camouflage uniforms as well, although I don't know what -- how many of them there were in percentages. Therefore, there were Arkan's men wearing black uniforms with the insignia including the tiger, and the Territorial Defence who wore those old olive-drab uniforms. And there were those who wore uniforms of darker green and they were members of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army. These uniforms were slightly different in the shade of the green that was a bit darker.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, the still from the meeting in the municipal hall is still displayed on your screen. Can you look at the soldiers in that still which is the still from Exhibit P589 and tell me whether you saw men dressed in the uniforms depicted in that still?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see this. Those are not the same uniforms. The uniforms I saw were pure black. In fact, no, the only uniform of that kind that I remember is one that I saw on the man who was standing at the entrance to the building of Radio Bijeljina. That was the only camouflage uniform I remember seeing. Maybe I have seen others, but I don't remember them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time that Arkan dismissed you from the municipal hall, do you recall what type of uniform he was wearing? And obviously we can --

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's this camouflage uniform. Sorry, that's the uniform on the man who turned me away. But I saw him later in a black uniform. I don't know when he had time to change but I also saw him in a black uniform, unlike this one, as we were returning from our visit to the hospital and from our door-to-door visits. I don't know really when they had time to change.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mr. Omeragic, just so that the Court is clear on this we've seen the video which depicts Arkan and the uniform he was wearing, and I'm asking you not to inform the Court what you saw in the video. But I'm asking you just to tell the Court about these events that took place in 1992, what you remember as being the uniform that Arkan was wearing, whether you remember it as being the uniform you've seen on the video or, alternatively, whether you remember it in a different way.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What sticks in my mind is that he was in a black uniform as I was following him two or three metres away. That's what I remember from that day. Whether they changed in the meantime, when and where, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Referring again to this photo which I see is the one you have on your left side and that has the number 08 in the top right-hand corner, the persons that appear to be victims are dressed in civilian clothes. Is this depiction consistent with information you received as to events that had taken place in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is consistent. All the information I received was information about people who had been killed, including some women.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the events outside -- and I've finished with that photograph exhibit and I'll now move on to the tour of the town. After the events outside the municipal hall, did you tour the town of Bijeljina and who -- and if so, who did you tour the town in the company of?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This delegation included Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Fikret Abdic, and Arkan. At the time, Arkan led the delegation. We went down a lane passing by a mosque, and we were going to the hospital to see wounded people, casualties, to visit them. I know that after a while, passing by some trees, we entered the hospital, and the delegation went into a ward. I couldn't see how large this ward was but I stopped at the door because there was a crowd already inside, then they moved to another ward, and in this way, they visited a couple of wards. Everybody would rush in following them, so I always somehow stayed behind. I wasn't able to come in. There was a young girl lying on one bed with a bandaged chest. I know where she was wounded, perhaps in the back. I said, "What happened you?" She was trying to say something, and I was trying to get her to relax, to talk to me. And she didn't seem able to say anything. I said, "Are you all right?" And she just mumbled something like, "I was wounded." I turned sideways just in time to see a uniformed man holding a gun and he seemed to be in complete control, these Arkan -- these men were in complete control of the situation. It was like the girl was looking at him and didn't dare say anything. Then we went into the building next to the hospital. Arkan asked, "This old lady who was killed, is she here?" We went into this apartment and I was told that some elderly woman, Mirjana Ilic, was killed there by a stray bullet. So we saw that scene. Again, men in black uniforms moved around. In this room, there was a huge coffin, the largest coffin I've ever seen. There were these men --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Not black uniforms but black suits. Black suits that are usually worn when somebody dies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a sign Gruhinic [phoen], a name plate, on the next door. And as we were knocking on that Gruhinic door, a young man ran out of the apartment next door, 27, 30 years old maybe, carrying a baby in his arms. And he said, very upset, "Look what's happening to us." He turned then to Fikret Abdic and said, "Just let it be peace." I asked the young man, "What's your name?" He said Mirza. And then he turned again to Fikret Abdic and said, "Let there be Serbia. Let there be anything. Just let there be peace so that my children can live." After that, we turned back towards the municipal hall. And at one point, Abdic asked to go into the mosque, the mosque that was in the park. Arkan said, "No problem."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've previously dealt with the issue of the mosque. If you could just continue on describing the events as you moved back towards the municipal hall, and also I would just like to remind you that we've also described the meeting with the journalist Vlado Mrkic. So if you could describe to the Court what occurred on the way back to the municipal hall and whether you spoke to any other people.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
