utterances.text: Between the hospital and the door-to-door visits, an elderly man, grey-haired, I believe he was completely toothless, approached us. His teeth were missing simply from old age. I don't think it was anything else. Anyway, this old man started talking about massacres, executions, people who were killed. He mentioned some specific people, I believe he mentioned an Albanian butcher, Sabanovic, then he mentioned some Dzevad Osmanovic who was also killed. The main thing he said was that they didn't spare any wounded people. They took no prisoners. And he seemed to trust me and started walking along with me for another 20 or 30 metres. And in that short interval of time, he managed to say a lot and to mention a lot of names that I tried to note down, the names of people who were killed. Sometime later, there was an exchange of fire, some shooting. Mr. Abdic and Mrs. Plavsic hid behind some garages, found shelter somewhere, and we were told that there was a sniper on top of the mosque. A couple of minutes later, I heard somebody radioing to Arkan that the sniper had been eliminated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, can I take you back to the hospital. Apart from your observation of the wounded girl, were you informed by Mr. Abdic or anybody else of any other wounded people that were in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember that. I really can't remember talking to Mr. Abdic about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you informed by anyone else as to whether or not anyone had been wounded either by gunshot or other means and whether they were in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I really can't recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to any doctors whilst you were at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This doctor was a plump man. He was yelling at people around, trying to usher the delegation into wards and at one point, I asked him, "Are there any wounded people to whom I could talk to, ask them how they were wounded?" He just gave me a short look, didn't say anything, and left. I really can't understand what it was all about, but I couldn't find out anything from him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, at any stage, visit Radio Bijeljina and, if so, what occurred upon that visit?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just after the visit to the hospital and the door-to-door visit and the arguing, we called on the Radio Bijeljina office. It had been announced that Fikret Abdic would be a guest in a live radio programme, talking to citizens. So Abdic and the others went upstairs and I didn't even try to go upstairs because I had learned my lesson by that time; I knew they wouldn't let me in. There was a guard standing at the door, a soldier. That soldier had a camouflage uniform on, for instance. There was a small portable radio by the soldier. I took that little radio and went upstairs to an empty room and sat down. There was a very big window in the partition wall, through which you could see the people inside the studio, and I could see that Mr. Fikret Abdic was talking to people on the telephone, but on the radio next to me all I could hear was music. I had worked in a radio station for a while in my career and I know that this music was supposed to be a background to fill in spaces between Mr. Abdic's talks with the citizenry, but instead of being a background, this music was all we could hear. Before that, Abdic, whenever I tried to tell him something, didn't really trust me. So I used this occasion to take this radio and to show it to Mr. Abdic's escort and to tell him, "Look, Mr. Abdic is talking to somebody on the phone now in a live radio programme, and you can't hear it on the radio." I returned the little portable radio to the owner after that, and that's all there was at the radio station. There was also a speech that Mr. Abdic was supposed to make which never took place. Some people later told me that they heard Mr. Abdic speak in the radio in Bijeljina, but I really can't understand what they heard in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to present the next exhibit to the witness and just to orient the witness to the examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd just like to remind you, Mr. Omeragic, that earlier in the course of your evidence we dealt a little bit out of chronological order, but we have dealt with the return to the municipal hall at the end of the tour and the conversations that you overheard between the various members of the delegation and also dealt with the farewell kiss between Arkan and Plavsic. And you've made observations to the Court, in particular in response to questions by His Honour Judge Hanoteau as to the relationship between various members or various persons present. In regard to this exhibit, I'd like to turn your attention to the fourth paragraph, and that's the first few sentences of the fourth paragraph. And just for certainty I'll read those into the record and they read as follows. This document is a daily operative report which is purportedly authored by General Savo Jankovic and dated 4 April 1992. And the fourth paragraph reads as follows: "The situation in the territory is extremely complex. The town of Bijeljina is controlled by the SDS and Arkan's men who do not even allow our anti-tank unit to reach certain positions in the town. There are about 3.000 refugees in the barracks and the cooperative hall area in Patkovaca. A team from the BH Presidency led by Fikret Abdic, Biljana Plavsic, the Chief of Staff of the 2nd Military District, and the commander of the 17th Corps has been in the Bijeljina barracks since 1200 hours." Mr. Omeragic, is this portion of the report consistent with your observations of which groups were controlling Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'd object to that question in terms of any inferences to be made from the evidence that the witness gives about who is controlling or not controlling, that's actually a matter for the Trial Chamber. To ask a question in relation to a document that the witness has never seen is consistent with your observations may, in some circumstances, be acceptable but not in circumstances where these fundamental issues of control are being looked at and the Trial Chamber is best served by forming its own conclusions from the available evidence rather than consistency or otherwise from the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts. I had -- just to shortcut matters, I had a few questions on it but I thought I'd wait in order not to interrupt you. On -- but I had some questions especially on that part of the testimony. I'll put it to the witness and then we'll see what's still needed. Mr. Omeragic, I'd like to put a few questions to you for further clarifications in respect of the crowd you described as being at the barracks. Could you tell us what was -- could you specify a sex of those who were in this crowd?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, those were mainly middle-aged or elderly women, children, and elderly men. There were no grown men, at least not that I could see. There were younger and slightly older women, children, and elderly men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That answered my second question which was about age. Third question: Did you observe anything that made it possible to you to identify the -- their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I really couldn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it could have been Serbs, Croats, Muslims, whatever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They could have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then did you gain an impression on whether they were free in their movements? Could they leave? Could they ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, just one thing about ethnicity. I heard General Jankovic say, "We have a mixed group here," whereas in another barracks in Patkovaca there were only Muslims, Bosniaks, and here we have Muslims and Serbs together. So General Jankovic explained at the time who the group consisted of. All I could see with my own eyes were frightened people. After all their terror, they fled to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They fled there. So is this an answer to my question whether they were free to go. They were not guarded in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, it's true there were people around who were armed, but they were not hostile in any way. Their barrels were pointed to the ground. They did not interfere in any way with the people. There could have been a total of 10 or 15 men from the JNA, soldiers, and I didn't think that they were keeping these people prisoners, on the contrary, they seemed to be protecting them. General Jankovic said also that they had given them shelter, fed them, and from all I could see, these people had fled to the barracks to find protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you testified that Fikret Abdic was saying that he wanted to meet with the refugees. I did not fully understand your testimony. I did understand that Fikret Abdic was with you. Did he consider this crowd not to be refugees or would they expect refugees to be somewhere else? It was not fully clear to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, those people fled their homes and they went to the barracks, which was perhaps 8 or 10 kilometres away. In my eyes, and I believe in Mr. Abdic's eyes, they were refugees because they fled their homes. I hope I understood your question correctly. If you were asking me about those refugees, in our language that means only one thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So when Mr. Abdic said, "I want to see the refugees," he was then confronted with what you considered to be and what he might have considered to be the refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Margetts, please proceed and let's see if there is any need for your last question, which was opposed by Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't see the need to pursue that last question, so I withdraw it. That said, of course, we are presenting that document as an exhibit, which is usefully considered in the context of this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, did you travel to Tuzla --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Madam Registrar, could you ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Prosecution Exhibit P590.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, following your visit to Bijeljina, did you travel -- actually I withdraw that question. At the start of your description of the tour of the town, you mentioned Fikret Abdic, Biljana Plavsic, and Arkan were in the group. Did you remain in their company for the duration of the tour of the town, including your visit to the hospital and the apartments?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was with them at the time when they went to the hospital, when they went on door-to-door visits. After that, Mr. Abdic went to Radio Bijeljina -- Semberija Majevica is another name for that radio station -- and after that, we went to the municipal hall or the Crisis Staff. It's the same building. Several things happened during that time. Outside the municipal hall, General Prascevic approached Arkan like a subordinate, Mrs. Plavsic kissed Arkan, then she suggested that he sort of hand over the control to the army because the town had been liberated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Omeragic, I believe we've dealt with those matters in your evidence. I just have one very specific question to follow-up on what you've previously informed the Trial Chamber, and it may already be implicit in your evidence if not entirely expressed, and that is, you referred to accompanying Abdic, Plavsic, and Arkan on the visits to various sites. As you moved between those sites and the various people spoke to you as you've described to the Court, were Abdic, Plavsic, and Arkan in your company at that time?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As these several things were going on outside the municipal hall, a lady showed up. She was just wearing trousers, track trousers, I believe --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apologies, I'm not dealing with the appearance of the lady or your presence outside the municipal hall. What I'm attempting to address with you is when you walked with the delegation between the municipal hall, the hospital, the apartment blocks and then back to the municipal hall, were you in the company of the delegation at that time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you answer the question; Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Thank you, Your Honour. This is the sort of generalised question that can't be answered in this way whilst the witness is in -- in my submission, whilst the witness is being taken through his evidence, sequentially, it's appropriate to ask who's there, who's not there, but to attempt to elicit a sort of cover-all in relation to presence in this way, in this leading fashion is, in my submission, not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the objection is overruled. The witness may answer the question. Perhaps, Mr. Margetts, you get the witness on the right track again, of course not even pushing any further, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I might be able to repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, His Honour has ruled that you may answer the question I put to you, which was this, and that is that: As you moved between the sites and the various people spoke to you, were Abdic, Plavsic, and Arkan in your company at that time?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was following them closely at a distance of about one metre, one metre and a half, and I was within earshot. I heard them talk about all manner of things. For instance -- or rather, I can't remember the details now, but from time to time, Arkan would say something about how he went to fight here and there and waged his battles, and then once Ms. Plavsic said in front of Mr. Abdic that Arkan's men had saved Serbs from becoming victims of crimes. I expected Abdic to react to this because, to say the least, the whole situation was very unclear and hazy. There was another peculiar thing that Arkan said. He asked Abdic whether he had ever been to Vukovar. Abdic replied that he hadn't. And then Arkan said, "This was something unforgettable for me." And this statement of his told me plenty about what his view of it all was. To him, wrecked and ruined houses were an unforgettable sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, after you left Bijeljina, you went to Tuzla and you had a meeting at the Tuzla JNA headquarters. Could you describe to the Trial Chamber who was present at that meeting and the conversations that took place at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We entered the headquarters of the 2nd Military District, there was General Jankovic and I believe General Prascevic. There was also Colonel Dubajic was who was reportedly commander of the barracks there, and a number of other lower-ranking officers up to the rank of majors. As we entered the compound and the building there, there was Ms. Plavsic and Mr. Abdic who sat in the first row, or rather, this was a rectangular table and that's how the seats were placed. There were also chairs placed along the walls. I sat in that back row to the right, and next to me there were JNA officers seated. I couldn't see all those seated at the table, but I could see General Jankovic and I believe at the table across from me, General Jankovic was seated. At one point, Ms. Plavsic started saying what she had previously been saying before Abdic, that the -- that Arkan's men had saved Serbs from their certain death because Muslims were preparing to commit a massacre on the day of Bajram. I reacted and said that this was not true. I told her, "Madam Plavsic, you should have gone there to see what was really happening there." I was presenting my opinion and said that the situation was the exact opposite of what she was saying. An altercation ensued, an exchange of exclamations, some of the officers there were saying something about the Second World War. I then said that they keep talking about World War II. There was an official report produced by Boguljub Kocevic for the UN immediately after World War II, and I said that according to that report, Jews were the greatest victim because 36 per cent of them perished, and they were followed by Bosnian Muslims of whom some 12 per cent perished and only then others followed. As I stated this, Ms. Plavsic, who seemed to be upset and disappointed, said, "Well, whose bones have we just been exhuming?" I told her, "Your people were also victims but Mr. Boguljub Kocevic who produced this official report for the United Nations which can still be found in the files there, clearly indicates how many victims there were among each of the ethnicities." Mr. Dubajic - I believe it was him because I recognised his voice - pointed with his finger, he motioned a small circle, and said, "Are you referring to a small area within Yugoslavia?" And I said, "No, I'm referring to all of Yugoslav territory." At that point, Mr. Abdic turned livid in the face and told me to shut up. I believe he was frightened by my remarks. Some other JNA officer made a joke or something, the meeting then ended, and as we went out, I looked over my shoulder and saw officers scurrying behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, can I stop you there. In terms of the meeting, did General Jankovic make any comments during the course of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That seems to me to be the most important point of the whole meeting. I was perhaps too daring in my remarks, and I said, "You should observe officers' honour and be sincere and say who it was that was the victim of fighting in Bijeljina, because it was Muslims who suffered most." I looked at General Jankovic and was shocked at hearing him say the following: "Yes, yes, Muslims. Muslims." He repeated "Muslims" twice. And I said, "Yes, Muslims." I was amazed at the fact that he admitted to what was actually true, that it was Muslims who were the victims of that situation, of that incident. And as I was dumbfounded by his admission, I went out to light a cigarette and then was joined by General Jankovic who approached me, outstretched his hand and clasped it then, shook my hand, and I was actually surprised at the strength of his fist. He told me, "You should not be that blunt, young man. That's for your own sake. You should take care of yourself because perhaps tonight you will have to enter into a war and God knows where that will lead us." My hand hurt from the firmness of his handshake. As the general was telling me this, I turned to his right where there was Ms. Plavsic. She was standing on the stairs, perhaps some 50 or 60 centimetres above us, at a distance of perhaps 1 or 2 metres on my left and on the general's right side, and she was looking straight at us. Her look showed an incredible amazement at what she had just seen; me and the general shaking hands. When the general saw me looking at Ms. Plavsic, he yanked his hand away and that's where we parted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, may I ask you, the question put to you was what comments Mr. Jankovic gave. We are under some time restraint. Although I do understand that you would like to tell us everything that what happened, would you please focus especially on the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we need further details, Mr. Margetts will certainly ask them. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Omeragic, for that description.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to present the final video clip to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The video will be Prosecution Exhibit P591 and the transcript will be P591A.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We asked for the former member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Dr. Biljana Plavsic, to comment on the statement by Alija Izetbegovic. Our colleague established a telephone link with Sarajevo just before the news bulletin started. This is their conversation. Plavsic: He was not there. Voice of reporter: Yes? Plavsic: Neither was I and I can't say anything but I must take this opportunity to mention a similar statement of his in connection with Bijeljina when on the eve of Bajram he spoke about the genocide against the Muslim people being perpetrated in Bijeljina. Voice of reporter: Yes? Plavsic: Mr. Fikret Abdic and I went to Bijeljina and saw that there was no question of any genocide committed against the Muslim people. In Bijeljina we saw snipers here and there. There were around 1.500 Kalashnikovs manufactured in Croatia which had been distributed there with which extremist Muslims, and the majority were Albanian, were supposed to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. carry out a pogrom of the Serbian population that night in Bijeljina. Bijeljina saved itself with an excellent organisation and preparations, and this is what Mr. Fikret Abdic and I had occasion to see. He focused even more attention so that he could convey the state of affairs to the Presidency and the republic as it was, and he had an opportunity to see that there were no incidents in which residents were killed. Those who died were killed by snipers who shot them. They were everywhere, at all elevated places in Bijeljina. For example, I don't know how many mosques Bijeljina has, but I tell you that they were in every mosque, on all high-rise buildings, and so forth. They had surrounded Bijeljina and were supposed to massacre the Serbian population. When we returned to Sarajevo and described the situation and I received a fax with a text on the entire situation, which was signed by more than 80 Muslims, refuting Izetbegovic's assertion, Izetbegovic did not say a thing. You know, he is a man who says something irresponsible and does not refer to that back any more. It was very important to get this across in order to raise the hatred of Serbs in Sarajevo to a boiling point. There, that was the objective of Izetbegovic's claim, and when we came, we were not given the chance to participate and speak in some broadcasts. Mr. Abdic was outraged over the fact that some of his statements were cut. He was not aware that Sarajevo television was already in the hands of Alija Izetbegovic."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, is what you observed on your visit to Bijeljina consistent with Plavsic's version of events as depicted in this video?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not notice any Kalashnikovs except for seeing now the green Kalashnikov that was mentioned, but I hadn't seen any at the time. I did not see any particular signs of fighting or 1.500 extremists. I really saw no signs of fighting. As for the presence of the snipers, there was this one incident involving the mosque that I've already told you about. I was just told that there was a sniper on top of the mosque, but that was all. I don't know anything about the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Omeragic, and thank you, Your Honour. That concludes the questions from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would like to put a question to you before you will be cross-examined by Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to come back to something now, something you said regarding the visit to Bosanski Brod. You said that while you were in the hall -- in the municipal hall, there was some shelling and you heard shooting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there was shelling and this involved Derventa. That was in Derventa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in Derventa. You said that Abdic and Mrs. Plavsic both used their phones to phone their friends in order to put an end to this shelling. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what they did. In that particular case, Ms. Plavsic called the officers at the barracks from where shells were being fired upon the town that had already been almost razed to the ground at the point. Mr. Abdic, on his part, called someone from the Crisis Staff of the HVO, Croatian Defence Council, that is to say, the Croat forces. The purposes of their phone calls were to make sure that the shelling stopped. In fact, it did stop, but then 10 minutes later, it was resumed as if nothing had transpired in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then you said in your testimony, [In English] "And I could see how powerful they were and what they could do about bringing about peace." [Interpretation] That's what you said before this Chamber. I'd like you to comment on that sentence. Could you be a little bit more explicit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was meant ironically. They have shown what their authority was. It lasted for 10 minutes and that was all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's how I had understood it. Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Abdic felt that they were there on some kind of mediation mission. Then shelling began, and they were very surprised because it's interfering with their mission. So they managed to get the shelling to stop and yet the shelling begins again 10 minutes later. So what you meant is that in truth, neither Mrs. Plavsic nor Mr. Abdic had any real authority or power over the troops, those who had begun the shelling. Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break now for 20 minutes. Mr. Usher, could you perhaps first escort the witness out of the courtroom because I've got one minor point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all in relation, Mr. Hannis, to Mr. Bjelobrk, may I take it that an e-mail that was sent by the Prosecution to the Defence of which the legal staff of this Chamber received a copy indicates that you leave it in the hands of the Chamber whether or not Mr. Bjelobrk will be ordered -- will be recalled for further cross-examination although you made some comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Unless you would like to add anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Margetts, I think that Madam Registrar is desperately trying to get the right description for some of your exhibits because not three of them, of course not all the three the same say that this is a clip from an interview with Arkan. Neither of the three contains an interview with Arkan, but I think Madam Registrar will find her way through that to see what it really shows. It might be that the overall omission was including a video of Arkan but at least a portion shown do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, would you like me to draft an appropriate description?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know how far Madam Registrar has got, but I think she would highly appreciate that at least that you offer to do so. We'll have a break until a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, you will now be cross-examined by Ms. Loukas, counsel for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Ms. Loukas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Omeragic. Now, Mr. Omeragic, just in relation to the evidence that you've given about the people in the barracks, the situation there is, of course, that as far as you were aware, the people in the barracks there were a mixed group; correct? And of course including Serbs, Croats, and Muslims; correct? Oh, I see. Your microphones are not on, Witness.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to your last two answers, I think --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'll just reconfirm them for the record, Your Honours, in view of the fact that there was no transcription.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there was no transcription after the first. But I think as a matter of fact that the answers given by the witness as it appears on the transcript now covers what the witness said, that he two times confirmed what you said, two times after you used the word "correct."

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour, yes. After the first time I said correct, he said yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And he again said yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: He again said yes, that's already recorded on the transcript. For the sake of the accuracy of the transcript, I think that's covered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, and these people had of course come to the JNA barracks to seek shelter; correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as far as you were concerned, Arkan and his units were establishing their own order in Bijeljina and the people there were seeking protection from the regular army; correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to events in the municipality prior to your arrival there on the 4th of April, and just going back to the evidence you gave when you were giving the evidence in the case against Mr. Milosevic, and that, the benefit for the Court and the Prosecution, is at page 27.697. You were asked some questions there about -- let's see: "Did you know that previously the Muslims had captured the town and were distributing weapons in the premises of the SDA and it was Alija Saracevic who was distributing those weapons?" And your answer was: "No, I know nothing about that." The next question was: "And do you know that they had set up sniper nests on the water tower and the Zitopromet Silo?" And your answer was: "No, I know nothing about that." You were then asked this question: "Didn't you inform yourself as to how these events had taken place in Bijeljina?" And your answer was: "You saw that I went to Bijeljina at the last moment, and I agreed to go to Bijeljina because I heard that there was a problem over there which I needed to explain, and I set off without any prior knowledge about these things that you are referring to." So I take it from your questions and answers there, Mr. Omeragic, that you're not in a position to give the Court any insight as to what was happening in Bijeljina prior to your arrival there; correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, may I just ask for one point of clarification, but it might by my incomplete understanding of the English language. If you're seeking protection from, does that mean that you want to be protected against or that you are seeking to be protected by?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I take that point. In fact, I was using the words actually from the Milosevic transcript, and I can perhaps clarify that. The words are, in fact, taken from 27700 and I can clarify it with the witness quite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I haven't got that. The only think I know is that the witness seemed to be quite clear in this respect in examination-in-chief, and I noticed that the first three questions, as a matter of fact, didn't do anything else than to seek confirmation of what the witness testified already in chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore, it's -- that's in evidence. I mean, if you want to mark things, we have discussed this before, after the third question, of course we are asking ourselves whether we get a repetition of what has been said in chief, and especially if you then move to another subject without giving any follow-up to that, then it's -- well, you have emphasised the importance of a certain portion. We don't need the witness for that, you can find other ways, as I said before, to draw our attention to -- I mean, it's quite clear there was a mixed group, and they are seeking -- at least this is how I understood it but I don't know what your question was about, but I understood the testimony of the witness in chief to be quite clearly that regular forces were surrounding them and they were protecting them.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So there's --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And it was a mixed group of Serbs, Muslims, and Croats, and they were seeking protection with the regular army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. All perfectly clear. No need --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: With and from the regular army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: With and from in the sense of the regular army was giving them protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Protecting against those who were establishing their own order.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well there's nothing new --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I don't think there's any question about those matters. I think we're all in agreement in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The question then is what's the need to have this all repeated. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, since there has been an interruption, it's a matter which I didn't wish to interrupt on, but having an opportunity to really look at the transcript properly, it probably is something that I should have interrupted. The quotations from the Milosevic transcript deal with very specific events. The question that has been then posed to the witness is a more general question as to whether he has any insight into what happened in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, let's be very brief. This Chamber has not received the Milosevic transcript, so we are totally unaware of it. It makes no sense to refer to that where the Chamber is not presented with it. This witness is produced as a viva voce witness and we received his earlier statement, but not as far as I remember any transcript in any other case. So don't expect any possibility for us to refer or to understand things better on the basis of the Milosevic transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But what you I am seeking is if Your Honour may be able to obtain clarification from Ms. Loukas as to when she says that the witness doesn't have insight into events, she was only referring to those events which she had quoted to the witness and not any other events in Bijeljina. Because I would understand from the way the question was put that was what was intended and that would have been what the witness intended in his response.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't think that Mr. Margetts can speak for what the witness intended in his response. I made two points. I referred the witness to his evidence in Milosevic and if I can just go to the portion of the transcript where I ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: That's page 65, lines 25, to page 66 line 2. And my point is that that question, I would say from -- the preamble to that question, should be constrained to the events which constitute the preamble.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, my question was very clear. I took the witness through what he had said in Milosevic then -- Your Honour, that was of course a preamble, appropriately so, and in cross-examination, I am entitled to ask the broader question and the witness has answered the broader question. That is my submission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, then I would seek clarification, either you may give me an opportunity to clarify it in re-examination, or Your Honour may wish to clarify it at this moment because it's now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will get an opportunity to clarify in re-examination. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we're at the point where prior to that interruption -- let me just check the point in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your question was about the insight as to what was happening in Bijeljina prior to your arrival there, and then the witness said "correct." Page 66, line 5, and then I interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Omeragic, I asked you this question: I take it from your questions and answers there, Mr. Omeragic, that you're not in a position to give the Court any insight to what was happening in Bijeljina prior to your appearance there; correct? And your answer was "Correct." So we're up to that point. Now, just in relation to that, clearly, you cannot offer the Court any direct knowledge of what occurred prior to your appearance there; correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your evidence is -- in relation to events that might have occurred prior to your arrival there is obviously something that you can only glean from conversations with people in the nature of hearsay; correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I hope we've clarified the point sufficiently for Mr. Margetts's purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may respond to that proposition from my learned friend. Insofar as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's really necessary to go through it again -- or I gave you an opportunity to further clarify. So for Ms. Loukas there was no need to ask whether it was sufficiently clarified because if you would consider it was not, then you have an opportunity to do so later. And I took it that Ms. Loukas was moving to her next subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed I am, Your Honour, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's then do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm just putting a marker there that it's inappropriate for Mr. Margetts to object during cross-examination to matters that are properly left to re-examination, and the cross-examination is going to take a very long time if we're subject to this sort of thing. That's why my marker was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, do you have any awareness of Muslim paramilitary formations in Bijeljina in late March, early April?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about in late March, early April, a bus station being damaged, any information on that?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Cafe Casina [phoen] belonging to Mirko Blagojevic, and a restaurant Belame [phoen] belonging to Ferad Zekovic [phoen] being destroyed?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of, on the 1st of April, 1992, in Bijeljina for approximately 24 hours an armed battle between armed Muslim groups and members of the Territorial Defence -- the local Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just in relation to the -- the name of the General Prascevic that you've mentioned. Are you certain that that's his name? Could there perhaps be a mistake in relation to his name? Could it be Brascevic you're talking about rather than Prascevic? Any information in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is Prascevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of -- on the 4th of April, people beginning to return to their homes, the people who had been -- some of the people who had been in the barracks, both Serbs and Muslims, beginning to return to their homes?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not. I didn't hear anything about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to your article, Mr. Omeragic, the information in your article in relation to Mauzer, that's of course wrong in your article, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in my article, I identified a man, as I said before, whom I mentioned earlier in my testimony, the one who threatened to drag me down to the ground floor of the municipal hall when this young man Peda interfered. And later, I identified on the photograph Ljubisa Savic, nicknamed Mauzer, who was some sort of local sheriff of the SDS down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to that, when did you make that identification. You've said "And later identified on the photograph, Savic." When did you make that identification?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe in 1997 in a copy of Slobodna Bosna newspaper which published the first interview with Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer, I saw the photographs in that article, and I remembered the young man with the bayonet who was hanging about the municipal hall. And it didn't take me long to remember him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So in that respect, in respect of the identification of Mauzer, you concede that your article was wrong; correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing is wrong with my article; it's just that I mistakenly identified in the article the man whom I later learned to be Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So your article is wrong in that respect, in respect of the identification of the wrong man. You agree with that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that part, the identification is incorrect; I agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the other aspect is this in relation to your article: There's a reference in your article to -- this is at page 3 for the benefit of the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber. At page 3, the English version, under your -- that heading, "Get Out!" what's contained there is that, "We sat there drinking raki for two full hours." Now, this aspect of "We sat there drinking raki" you say is not correct; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I now heard some switch. It seems that I do not receive any more the French translation on the English channel. Could you please repeat your question to the witness, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Your Honour. I should indicate for the record that I'm referring to the article that's as an Exhibit P584. I will just find my question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you look for it, I'll put the question to the witness again. Ms. Loukas asked you as follows: "Now, the other aspect is this in relation to your article ... there's a reference in your article to -- that heading 'Get Out!' what's contained there is that, 'We sat there drinking raki for two full hours.' Now, this aspect of, 'We sat there drinking raki' you say is not correct; is that right?" That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not right, and if I may be allowed to explain, Your Honour. When I returned to Sarajevo, if I may first of all say that in the corridor outside the room where talks were held from which I was barred, I spent some 35 minutes there, not more. That much is true. On my return to Sarajevo, there was already a war on. I had to run to and fro under sniper fire, I was writing my article, and as I interrupted my writing of the article for a moment, my editor sat down at the desk and checked what I had written up to then, and then together with the lady journalist who worked there in the editorial office there, he said -- "And you were drinking raki for a full two hours." He liked those kinds of jokes. He added these words because he perceived them as a joke. He thought that as I was going to sit back at my desk, I was going to find that funny. However, what happened was that I never even checked whether anything had been added to my text, I just went on writing and this bit remained in the text. How could I have drunk anything for a full two hours when I was only there for 35 minutes? I did not have occasion to review my article after I had written it or else I would have corrected that bit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people you've indicated there, your editor, what's his name?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Senad Avdic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the lady journalist you've referred to?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Susanna Jotanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you say your editor inserted, "We were drinking raki for two hours"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could in the have written it myself in reference to a place where I spent a mere 35 minutes, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you drinking raki for 35 minutes?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe a bottle of raki was circulated round. I may have taken a sip, but I do not really -- spirits don't really sit well with me. I can't stand the drink.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your editor apropos of nothing, it's not in your article, says you were sitting around drinking raki for two hours. Is that what you're telling the Court?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're telling the Court that the editor of your newspaper inserts you drinking raki into your article. That's precisely what you're saying, is it?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope I don't have to repeat this. He did this to others as well. He regarded it as some sort of a joke because people would usually notice it, but I did not. He did this to my colleague, Manuel Tomkovic. He'd write a sentence, a line, and then would just leave it there or maybe make a phone call to that effect. However, I was never aware of this joke played on me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you read the article after it was printed?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course your newspaper, like newspapers around the world has provisions for corrections. Did you correct the article?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. If you wish me to provide an explanation for that, I can. We did not have enough paper to print Slobodna Bosna, and in fact no further issues were published. We were to print the paper only seven or eight months later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And in relation to Slobodna Bosna, and in particular your article, was there anything else your editor inserted into the article as a joke?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. How about subsequent copies of Slobodna Bosna after it started being printed again? Any more jokes in Slobodna Bosna from your editor?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know because I no longer worked for Slobodna Bosna. After its printing was resumed, only two or three more issues were published because the conditions made it impossible. As for the selling of the paper, I have to tell you that I myself went out in the streets of Sarajevo to sell the paper because with the shelling and everything, nobody dared to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to your article again. Again, this is at page 3 of your article, the exhibit number being P584, under the heading "Arkan Takes No Wounded" this portion appears, "A person approached me and whispered (desperate because I was not allowed to tape, I tried to remember everything)..." Now this, of course, is critical for journalists, is it not, to take notes at the time when they are gathering material for an article; correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it when you left the hospital you took down notes of what had occurred at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did manage to make notes of some things but I cannot tell you precisely of what because more than ten years have elapsed since, but I did manage to make a note or two, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it you still have those notes today?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't. I do not have them as -- I don't have keepsakes at all, not the ones dating from before the war. I have lost everything, just as many other people have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were asked by the Prosecution to give a statement in relation to events surrounding your article - and this interview was taken of course in August 2001 you will recall, and that of course is some nine, almost ten years after the events in question - did you have any notes of your own in relation to those events that had occurred almost ten years earlier?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have notes of any sort. I didn't even have the article that I had written. I tried to remember everything I could at that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you only had the article to go on in terms of notes when you gave your statement to the Prosecution; correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall having the article, but yes, I might have been given the article to refresh my memory. And as for notes, of course, I didn't have any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to your specific references to Mrs. -- Dr. Biljana Plavsic in the article --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: If the witness might be shown the article, P584.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, your specific references to Ms. Plavsic, firstly under the headings, "The victims," and you've got, "Dr. Biljana Plavsic, who recently said in public that far more Serbs than Muslims had lost their lives." All right. That's one reference to Ms. Plavsic. There's a second reference to Mrs. Plavsic under "Ring around the refugees," in the second paragraph. There you are to go right away to the municipality hall where Mrs. Plavsic is waiting. You are about to meet with Arkan. The next reference to Mrs. Plavsic is "Mrs. Plavsic appealing to Arkan to allow the army to take over the town." And that is under the heading, "Exit from hell." And the following reference just a little further down, "Mrs. Plavsic is interviewed by Ekspres Politika thanking Arkan for his intervention. She kisses Arkan good-bye." And then under "Unforgettable Vukovar." Now, I take it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, did you intend to refer to all the references to Dr. Plavsic, then you might have forgotten one on page 1 of the English translation, fourth line from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh indeed, Your Honour. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with that correction from His Honour, they are basically all your references to Mrs. Plavsic; correct? Anything else you say about her in your article?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, firstly, apart from conceding that the article is wrong in relation to Mauzer and the reference to you drinking raki for two hours, I take it you stand by your article firstly as true and accurate; correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course you also stand by the statement you've given to the Prosecution as true and accurate; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in addition to this text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in relation to how you compile an article as a journalist, obviously number one is to ensure accuracy; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, could you come to your point, please? There seems to be some inconsistency or something like that, and that's in the air already for the last three minutes. Let's get to the point.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I understand that, but classically in cross-examination the advocate is allowed to -- and I shouldn't be saying this in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I know that the classical cross-examination includes --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Includes closing the gates, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm aware of that. The Chamber is in a position that to assess whenever someone tries to find an escape route, what the value of such an escape route would be. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, and you also, of course -- one fundamental issue in relation to producing a story is of course newsworthiness; correct? That's a priority, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you have the theory of journalism in mind?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you. Isn't one of your priorities in producing an article, and you prioritise the matters that you put in that article, newsworthiness?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, what matters is the news, the information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exactly. And what are your priorities for newsworthiness?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My priority is to write about what I saw, about what I was able to observe and to fathom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but obviously you see a lot, so in terms of working out what you're going to put in the article and what you leave out of the article, what are your usual priorities?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, the question is at such a level of obstruction that it certainly would help the witness, I take it, that you make it more concrete because a journalist, on average, could speak easily for one hour on priorities in newsworthiness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: There's no doubt about that, Your Honour, but this witness doesn't seem to be able to speak about it at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is someone sticking a gun in your face newsworthy?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You're right. Your Honours, I can also explain this: Why some of the things that I testified to have not been published in my article. Whenever I work on a piece of writing, I try to avoid placing myself at the forefront of things. I didn't want to present myself as an important person, and that's the reason why. Later on, when I gave my testimony, I was the witness and that's why I presented things differently, whereas in my article, I did not wish to place myself in the forefront. It was Bijeljina, the town itself and the events there, that were in the forefront. It is not that I was unable to write things this way. It was just a matter of choice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about you asking a Territorial Defence member, "Did you cut down those balijas?" and his response being, "Yes, we have killed quite a lot of them." Do you think that's newsworthy?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not in your article either, is it?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there is one section where I write about it, in the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Later on, the same thing was told to me by a man wearing a band around his arm about the 25 bodies. A fighter with a ribbon on his shoulder repeated the information and appeared to be proud of it." And I'm referring to the 25 corpses that I heard about on the radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, would you agree with me that's a pretty important conversation. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's pretty newsworthy to put in those quotes, isn't it? To put it in precisely and accurately as a journalist. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it was up to me to present things my way and I opted for this way and I did it this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't think --

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been qualified later on as some sort of an exaggeration of what had actually transpired as extortion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As extortion, Mr. Omeragic? What do you mean by "extortion"?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For instance, just as you qualified the questions put by the Prosecutor as "leading questions," I put a leading question and that was how I came by that piece of information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, you're a journalist. Journalists are entitled to do that. You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't understood you. What is it that I'm entitled to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, I understood the testimony of the witness to be just that where he elicited the information from his source, that that could be misunderstood as that he -- I mean, what's the problem with leading questions is that you suggest something that might not be true. If you understand it that way, then a journalist might find reasons to just present the information and not the way it was asked to his source. And it's really not a matter to be explored in full detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there are obvious differences between being in a courtroom and being a war correspondent, and the rule of leading questions tends not to apply in war journalism, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No one, no one will ever argue that it would apply. And therefore I invite you to listen to the witness and try to understand what he says, which is that he explained why he did not put the way he asked for the information but that he just put the essence of the information in his article.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I will move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Loukas, it's 17 minutes to 2.00, and I have one decision still to read. So therefore, I'd rather stop, if this is the suitable moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you lead the witness out of the courtroom after I have instructed him -- no, could you please -- I said after I instructed you that you should speak to no one about your testimony, the testimony you have given or you are still about to give, and we would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this same courtroom. Yes. Thank you, Mr. Omeragic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The decision I'd like to deliver is a decision on Prosecution's motion for protective measures for Witnesses 31 and 73. The motion which is partly confidential was filed on the 11th of March, 2005. The motion also refers to one other witness who has already testified under protective measures. Pursuant to Rules 75 and 79, the Prosecution requests the Chamber to order the use of pseudonyms when referring to these witnesses as well as image and voice distortion during their testimonies. The motion also requests private session but only for those portions of their testimonies which are likely to reveal their identities. In its motion, the Prosecution relies, in part, on a recent UNHCR report relating to the current security situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The report also mentioned Bosnia and Herzegovina's inability to ensure the safety of witnesses. In the confidential annex to the motion, the Prosecution sets out specific details relating to the protective measures sought for Witnesses 31 and 73. In its response dated the 8th of April, 2005, the Defence requests that the Chamber decline to rule on the motion until the Prosecution has produced all information relevant to an overall assessment of the circumstances justifying protective measures. The Defence also states that the current security situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina does not, of itself, justify the granting of protective measures. The law on protective measures has been stated by this Chamber in recent decisions. The Chamber is mindful that a fair and a public hearing is a right of the accused and is in the interests of justice. Measures concealing the identity of a witness should be granted only in limited circumstances. It must be shown that should it become publicly known that the witness has testified, there is a real risk the existence of which is supported by some objective evidence to the security of the witness or his or her family. The threat made to the witness is usually a sufficient basis to grant protective measures but the existence of a threat is not necessary. The Chamber considers that the requisite objective foundation for the risk may also be demonstrated through such circumstances as a combination of the following three factors: 1: The expected testimony of the witness may antagonise persons who continue to reside in the territory in which the crimes were committed. For example, by implicating those persons in crimes. 2: The protective witness or his or her family live in that territory, have property in the territory, or have concrete plans to return to live in the territory. 3: A general security situation which is unstable and is particularly unfavourable to witnesses and the families of witnesses who appear before the Tribunal. Under such circumstances which are present for Witness 31 and 73, the Chamber may order appropriate protective measures. It should be emphasised this is only one way to establish the existence of an objectively-granted risk to the security of a witness. When assessing the likelihood of danger or risk to prospective witnesses, the Chamber will take into consideration all relevant factors, including any threats made against the witness and the position of the witness in the community. The Chamber has considered these submissions of the parties in relation to the present motion, evaluating them in the light of the climate in Bosnia and Herzegovina which is set out in the UNHCR report remains unfavourable to persons who are resident there or have family resident there and who wish to fully discharge their duty to testify before the Tribunal. The Chamber considers that the testimonies of Witnesses 31 and 73 which will likely implicate local Serbs from the areas in which the witnesses reside -- I was not very clear -- will likely implicate local Serbs from the areas in which the witnesses reside in serious crimes may antagonise persons living in those areas exposing the witnesses to a risk of retaliation. The Chamber therefore considers that the Prosecution has established that these witnesses would be exposed to a real security risk if it became known that they had testified. The Chamber finds that the requested protective measures, that is, pseudonym, image and voice distortion, as well as limited use of private session, strike a balance between the need to protect Witnesses 31 and 73 and the accused's right to a public trial. The motion, therefore, is granted. Before I adjourn, Ms. Loukas, could you give us any indication as to the time you would need for cross-examination, further cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would have thought it would take me up to the first break, I should imagine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is -- would be two and a half against --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't think I've had an hour this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you started cross-examination close to 1.00. We resumed at five minutes to 1.00, and I think that you went on until 1.43. That would be 50 minutes. If you would take one more one hour and a half, that would bring you to -- yes, approximately two hours and 20 minutes where the -- I think that the Prosecution took approximately three and a half hours, if I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I think it was a little bit more than that, actually, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll look --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Ms. Philpott is shaking her head. I'm sure we have the exact calculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can obtain them from the registry. Especially looking at the start of your cross-examination, Ms. Loukas, where, as I said before, the first of three questions, it really did not add any one single scintilla to what was said in chief. The Chamber is inclined to take the guidance of the 60 per cent rather strictly.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I understand that. But to be interrupted three minutes into one's cross-examination when an advocate is entitled to put matters that are favourable to a particular analysis of a situation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both parties have taken their time to interrupt, and we'll -- during this afternoon and overnight, we'll consider whether there was any significant difference in the way the other party was interrupted and objections were put to the other party. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
